title: PM asks COP31 to put half of climate finance into adaptation
excerpt: In Bangladesh's national statement, Tarique Rahman set out five proposals, including debt relief and grants instead of loans.
content:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman called for at least half of international climate finance to go to adaptation, in Bangladesh’s national statement to the High-Level Segment of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Thursday, 12 November, The Business Standard reported.

“Climate-vulnerable countries need grants, not more loans that increase their debt,” he said.

The five proposals

  1. At least 50% of international climate finance for adaptation, guided by each country’s priorities, while still supporting emissions cuts.
  2. Debt relief, including debt-for-climate swaps and climate-resilient debt clauses.
  3. Fair access to climate-friendly technologies and support for their transfer to developing countries.
  4. Faster moves to renewable energy through affordable finance, skills training and a fair energy transition.
  5. Adoption of the Belém-Antalya Action Mechanism for a just transition at COP31, with fair finance and fair trade at its core.

What Bangladesh says it will do

  • Generate 20% of electricity from renewables by 2030, including 4,000 MW of solar power supported by special tax incentives.
  • Plant 250 million trees over five years.
  • Excavate 20,000 km of rivers and canals.

He said Bangladesh produces less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The newspaper did not report a cost or timeline for the domestic plans.

Where the talks stand

The 50% ask goes further than Bangladesh’s earlier call to triple adaptation finance. It sets a share of all climate finance, not just an amount. UN Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders on 11 November that global emissions must fall by about 6% a year and that current national plans deliver at best a third of that, according to UN Climate Change. The EU has said there is little political will for new finance pledges at this COP.

Why it matters

Most of the climate work NGOs do in Bangladesh, from coastal embankments to flood early warning and salinity-tolerant farming, is adaptation. A larger adaptation share, paid as grants, would mean more money that can reach local organisations without adding to national debt. The tree-planting and canal excavation plans may also bring partnership work for local NGOs and community groups.

What to watch

  • Whether the 50% share or a tripling baseline appears in a draft decision text on adaptation finance.
  • Whether the just transition mechanism Bangladesh backs is adopted before COP31 closes.
  • Details, costs and implementing agencies for the 250 million trees and 20,000 km of canals.
